title: Your coding agent doesn't always follow your rules — Talha Sheikh, Checkout.com
talk_summary: Speaker argues coding agents are capable but unreliable, so instructions alone are insufficient; he built a hook-triggered deterministic verification harness that checks outputs and feeds failures back for retries. He generalizes this to a language-agnostic contract/verification layer at multiple lifecycle points, claiming stronger guardrails can let teams use cheaper models and should pace work to verification capacity.

takeaways.what_they_do: On agent session end, a hook runs config-defined deterministic checks; failures are returned to the agent to retry until checks pass.
takeaways.evidence_quote: whenever Claude finishes its its session, it automatically the hook calls my vector product or program, and then it checks it for me

takeaways.what_they_do: Acceptance criteria are executable checks rather than prose rules the agent may ignore.
takeaways.evidence_quote: instructions is not the same thing as giving it verification

takeaways.what_they_do: Invest in verification harness so smaller/open models can be routed to tasks with strong checks; reserve frontier models for ambiguous work.
takeaways.evidence_quote: you can use a smaller model like a Haiku or even like an open source models because it's got these guardrails on

takeaways.what_they_do: Run checks at conversation end, pre-commit, multi-agent handoff, async completion, and optionally LLM judge.
Treat verification as bottleneck; don't let agent generation outrun checks/reviews.
takeaways.evidence_quote: it's because the verification layer. You need to verify that everything is working or not

takeaways.technique: LLM judge as layered feedback loop
takeaways.what_they_do: Use nondeterministic LLM judge as one check among deterministic gates, feeding findings back to agent.
takeaways.evidence_quote: you can have a check that nondeterministically calls like um LLM an LLM as a judge sort of a thing
